source: Holton, Mackridge & Philippaki-Warburton, Greek: An Essential Grammar, 2nd ed. (Routledge, 2016), upload 7635aa83 (PDF pp. 26-50 = Ch 1, Ch 2, §3.1-3.2). Copyrighted, no open license stated: rules are restated in our own words, examples limited to single words and short phrases.

alphabet.name: γάμα
alphabet.sound: ɣ before a/o/u/consonant; j before e/i

alphabet.name: σίγμα
alphabet.sound: s (z before voiced consonant); ς only word-final

vowels.note: Spelling is fully predictive for reading but not for writing: one sound /i/ has six spellings.

digraphs.double_consonants: Doubled letters are pronounced as one (γράμμα [ɣráma], αλλά [alá]); the only exception is γγ = (ŋ)g.

rules.rule: π, τ, κ are never aspirated, even word-initially (like English 'spot', 'stay', 'scot').
κ, χ, γκ/γγ become palatal [k'], [x'] (h in 'huge'), [g'] before /e/ and /i/; γ before /e/, /i/ is [j] (y in 'yes').
σ is [z] before a voiced consonant (β, γ, δ, μ, ν, ρ).
ν is [ŋ] before /x, ɣ, k, g/ and [ɲ] (ni in British 'new') in ν + unstressed ι + vowel.
λ + unstressed ι + vowel gives palatal [l'].
Unstressed ι (any /i/ spelling) before a vowel loses syllable status: [j] after a voiced consonant, [x'] after a voiceless one; formal/learned words keep it syllabic.
Vowels can stand side by side (νεαρός [nearós]); unstressed ι after a vowel forms a diphthong-like [oi], [ai], [ei] (ρολόι, πάει, λέει).

consonant_clusters.note: Up to three consonants word-initially, four word-internally. These initial clusters do not exist in English.
consonant_clusters.three_note: Complete: the book lists only these three initial three-consonant clusters absent from English (confirmed 2026-10-17 against the text-layer copy, 'Essential Greek part 1').

colloquial_vs_formal.rule: Many words have a colloquial cluster (fricative + stop) and a formal one (two fricatives or two stops). Colloquial form in speech, formal in writing.

sandhi.scope: Within phrases: article + word, weak pronoun + verb, δεν/μην + verb, preposition + its object.

rules.rule: Final ν (τον, την, δεν, μην) + initial π: π → [b], ν → [m] or dropped.
Final ν + initial τ: τ → [d], ν may drop.
Final ν + initial κ: κ → [g], ν → [ŋ] or dropped; after [g] a following σ (in ξ) voices to [z].
Final ς of an article, weak pronoun or ας → [z] before a voiced consonant.

The final ν of feminine την (article and pronoun) and of μην is usually dropped in speech and writing before a word starting with a fricative, σ, ζ, λ, ρ, μ, ν; kept before vowels and stops. The masculine τον always keeps ν in writing.
A weak pronoun or particle ending in a vowel may lose it (or the verb may lose its initial vowel) before a vowel; written with an apostrophe and a space.
το/τα may drop their vowel before a word beginning with /a/.
σε + definite article contracts obligatorily: σε + το → στο, σε + την → στην, etc. από optionally elides: απ' την.
A two-syllable perfective imperative may drop final ε before a neuter weak pronoun or article.

rules: Every word of two or more syllables has one stressed vowel (higher pitch, slightly longer and louder).
Stress falls on one of the last three syllables only (ultimate, penultimate, antepenultimate): αγαπητός, ταχυδρόμος, άγριος.
Adjectives keep the stress on the same syllable in all forms.
In some noun classes stress shifts right in the genitive: μάθημα → μαθήματος, μαθημάτων; δάσκαλος → δασκάλου, δασκάλων; θάλασσα → θαλασσών.
In some verbs the stress moves left in past tenses: σπουδάζω → σπούδαζα. If an ending would leave three unstressed syllables at the end, stress moves right: δέχομαι → δεχόμαστε.

enclisis.rule: When a word is followed by weak pronouns (verb + object pronouns, noun/adjective + possessive, adverb + pronoun) and its stress would end up more than three syllables from the end of the group, a second stress goes on the second syllable to the right of the original one. Both stresses are written.

intonation.contour: rises, then falls slightly to mid level at the end
rises and stays high at the end
falls at the end, then immediately rises
normally the last stressed word of the verb phrase carries the peak; a fronted emphasized element gets a rise then fall (contrast, surprise)

accent.system: Monotonic (one accent mark), taught in schools since 1982.
rules: Write an acute accent on the stressed vowel of every word of more than one syllable.
Initial capital: accent goes before the letter (Όμηρος). Words in all capitals take no accent.
Two-letter vowel (ου, αι, ει, οι) or αυ/ευ: accent on the second letter (τοίχος, παύω).
If the two letters are pronounced as separate vowels, accent the first when it is stressed (γάιδαρος).
Enclisis: write both accents (ο εξάδελφός μου).
One-syllable words normally take no accent, except: words shortened by elision (φέρ' το); ή 'or' vs article η; question words πού, πώς vs relative/complementizer που, πως.
Recommended: accent a weak pronoun object of the following verb when it could be misread as a possessive: Η μητέρα μού είπε 'Mother told me' vs Η μητέρα μου είπε 'My mother said'.
Ordinal numerals as capitals take a keraia: Γεώργιος Β΄.

diaeresis.rule: ¨ on the second of two vowels shows they are pronounced separately (γαϊδάρου). Not needed when the first vowel is accented (γάιδαρος). On a stressed vowel both marks combine (καΐκι).

apostrophe.rule: Marks a deleted vowel; the words stay separated by a space (θα 'ρθω, θ' ανέβω).

rules: Capital at sentence start and for names of people, places, days, months and religious festivals.
Words derived from such names usually take lower case: ένας Έλληνας but η ελληνική μουσική.
Titles before names are lower case: η κυρία Μητσάκη.
Book titles: capital on first word only or on every word; both occur.

marks.name: διπλή τελεία / άνω και κάτω τελεία
παύλα
marks.en: dash; also introduces each speaker in dialogue

differences_from_english: Full stop in abbreviations (π.χ.), clock times (11.40) and thousands (1.234.567).
ό,τι 'whatever' is written with a comma to distinguish it from ότι 'that'.
Question mark is ; and semicolon is ·.
Direct speech: either a dash per speaker or «» quotes.

orthography.foreign_names: No fixed standard. Some are naturalized and inflect (ο Δαρβίνος, η Οξφόρδη), some follow pronunciation (ο Μπους, το Λος Άντζελες), older ones compromise with spelling (Καίμπριτζ); simplified spellings (Κέμπριτζ) are recommended but contested. Names without an established form are often left in Latin script.
